LESSON 10 OF 106·Networking Fundamentals

DNS: Turning Names into Addresses

What DNS actually does, how an uncached lookup travels through the hierarchy, why caching changes everything, and how the same mechanism becomes an attack surface.

Beginner14 min
Why this matters

DNS turns names into addresses. It is the first request almost every session makes, and because it is trusted implicitly, an attacker who can answer it can redirect a user without breaking TLS.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A resolver asks a recursive server on your behalf, and that server walks the hierarchy from the root to the top-level domain to the authoritative server.
  • Records carry the answer: A records for IPv4, AAAA for IPv6, CNAME for aliases, MX for mail, and TXT for verification and policy.
  • Answers are cached with a time to live, so a change does not take effect everywhere immediately.
  • A typical lookup is plain UDP, which is fast and easy to spoof because there is no built-in authentication.
  • DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to records so a validating resolver can detect a forged answer, and it must be used at every step of the chain.

The background

  • DNS replaced a single hosts file so that name changes did not require manual updates across a network.
  • The original design trusted resolvers completely, which is why cache poisoning has been a productive attack for as long as it has existed.
  • Later additions covered mail, service discovery and verification, so the same system is now load-bearing for far more than browsing.
  • Encrypted transports such as DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS reduce tampering on the hop between client and resolver.

Real-world examples

  • An attacker who spoofs a DNS answer can send a user to a lookalike site even when the address bar shows the expected domain, because the request never reached the real host.
  • Expired registrations on internal service subdomains have repeatedly been used to claim internal names and redirect traffic.
  • A stale cache after a migration sends some users to an old server for as long as the old time to live allows.

What to look for

  • Check the resolver being used, since an unexpected resolver means someone else sees every lookup.
  • Notice DNS answers that point at unfamiliar hosting or at addresses in unexpected ranges.
  • Review internal records for names that could be claimed externally.
  • Prefer TLS for resolver traffic on networks you do not control.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Pin resolver traffic with DNSSEC validation where possible.
  • Encrypt resolver traffic with DNS over HTTPS or DNS over TLS.
  • Keep the time to live low on records you may need to change, and high only where you control the risk.
  • Register internal-looking names defensively, and monitor for unexpected changes to public records.
